title: Latitude and Longitude: Finding Places on Earth
summary: How an invisible grid of latitude and longitude lines lets anyone give any spot on Earth its own exact set of numbers, and how GPS uses that grid today.
poll: I could find my own city on a globe using only latitude and longitude numbers.

versions.title: Lines That Find Places
versions.text:
Earth is big. We need a way to find one spot on it. People draw lines on a map. The lines make a grid.

Some lines go side to side. We call them latitude lines. They tell how far north or south you are. The middle line is the equator.

Other lines go up and down. We call them longitude lines. They tell how far east or west you are.

Each line has a number. Two numbers can name one spot. No other spot has the same two numbers.

Long ago, sailors looked at stars. Stars helped find one of the numbers. The other number was much harder to find.

Today we use GPS. GPS talks to satellites. It finds your spot fast.

On a globe, lines cross each other. Each cross is one small square. Each square is one spot on Earth.

Maps use this grid. Ships use it too. Planes use it to fly right.

The equator sits at zero degrees latitude, exactly between the top and bottom, while the poles sit at ninety degrees.

Lines of longitude, by contrast, stretch from the North Pole to the South Pole, intersecting every latitude line along the way. Each longitude line is also called a meridian, and it measures how far east or west a place lies. One meridian, the prime meridian, was officially chosen in 1884 to represent zero degrees, running through Greenwich, England.

Every place on Earth, no matter how remote, can be described using its own unique pair of coordinates. Because no two places ever share the same pair, these numbers work much like a permanent address written in degrees.

For centuries, navigators studied the stars and the sun to estimate their latitude fairly well. Longitude proved far harder to measure, because it required an extremely precise clock, called a chronometer, able to keep correct time while rocking at sea for months.

On a globe, lines of latitude and lines of longitude intersect everywhere, forming a grid that closely resembles graph paper wrapped around a sphere. Each intersection marks one exact spot on the planet.

Lines of longitude, by contrast, extend from the North Pole all the way to the South Pole, intersecting every latitude line along their circuitous path around the circumference of the globe, and each longitude line, also called a meridian, quantifies how far east or west a particular place lies in relation to a fixed reference, namely the prime meridian, officially designated in 1884 to represent zero degrees and running directly through Greenwich, England, with every other meridian measured as an angular distance east or west of it, up to one hundred eighty degrees, where east and west converge.

Every place on Earth, however remote or inaccessible, can be characterized using its own unique pair of coordinates, frequently subdivided further into minutes and seconds for additional, finer-grained precision, and because no two places ever share the identical pair, these numbers function much like a permanent address expressed entirely in degrees rather than in conventional street names.

Upon a globe, lines of latitude and lines of longitude intersect ubiquitously, forming a grid that closely resembles graph paper stretched tightly around a sphere, and each intersection demarcates one exact, unrepeatable spot somewhere on the entire planet, irrespective of its distance from any city, road, or coastline.

Modern maps, ships, airplanes, and even ordinary smartphones all depend heavily upon this identical coordinate grid, since it enables navigators and everyday travelers alike to find their way safely toward whatever destination they choose, with a degree of navigational precision that earlier sailors could scarcely have imagined possible within their entire lifetimes.

options: It talks to satellites to work out its latitude and longitude
It builds brand new roads across the land for cars and trucks
It prints fresh paper maps for travelers on a long trip
It slowly changes where the equator is located on the Earth
questions.why: The article says a GPS receiver talks to satellites and finds its own latitude and longitude quickly.

wrong.B: Roads are not built by GPS devices.
wrong.C: Printing maps is not described.
wrong.D: The equator's location does not change.

questions.stem: In the article, the word navigator most nearly means —
options: a person who studies only the weather
a person who draws pictures for a living
a person who constructs very tall buildings
a person who finds the way from place to place
questions.why: The article discusses old sailors and navigators finding their way using latitude and longitude.

wrong.A: Studying weather is unrelated to navigating.
wrong.B: Drawing is not the meaning of navigator.
wrong.C: Building is not related to navigating.

questions.stem: Why was finding longitude at sea so difficult for old sailors?
options: Paper maps had simply not been invented yet in those years
It required an extremely accurate clock, which was hard to build
There were far too many fish swimming nearby, so ships were slow
Sailors were not permitted to look at the stars at night
questions.why: The article explains that finding longitude needed a clock accurate enough to work on a rocking ship.

wrong.A: Maps are discussed throughout the article.
wrong.C: Fish are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Stars were used to help find latitude, not forbidden.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a pilot rely on GPS rather than stars?
options: Because stars are always more accurate than any GPS
Because airplanes are physically unable to see satellites
Because GPS does not work at all over open water
Because GPS gives exact coordinates quickly, even through clouds
questions.why: The article shows GPS calculates exact location within seconds, which is more reliable than depending on visible stars.

wrong.A: The article presents GPS as the more precise modern method.
wrong.B: Airplanes use GPS, which depends on satellites.
wrong.C: GPS is shown working almost anywhere, including over oceans.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why every place needs its own unique coordinates?
options: So that oceans never need any coordinates at all
So that places can change location whenever they choose
So that only large, famous cities appear on maps
So that any location can be told apart from every other
questions.why: Since no two places share the same pair, the unique coordinates let every spot be clearly identified.

wrong.A: Oceans have latitude and longitude too.
wrong.B: Locations stay fixed; their coordinates do not change.
wrong.C: Even remote, non-city places get coordinates.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: It compares the flags used by different countries at sea for many years
It lists the dangers of ocean travel in time order, one storm after another
It tells a long story about a single sailor's journey
It explains each line, then how they work together, then their history
questions.why: The article moves from explaining latitude, to longitude, to coordinates, to history, to today's GPS use.

wrong.A: Flags are not discussed.
wrong.B: Dangers of travel are not the focus.
wrong.C: No single sailor's story is told.

MID.prompt: Explain how a GPS receiver finds an exact location. Use the words satellite and coordinate.
checklist: I explained how GPS uses satellites.
I explained what a coordinate is.
I used evidence from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: A GPS receiver communicates with a network of satellites circling Earth, and using signals from several of them, it calculates its own exact coordinate, meaning its precise latitude and longitude. This lets the device find its location within seconds, which is much faster than the methods sailors once used, such as studying the stars.

keyWords.definition: a line of longitude running from pole to pole
keyWords.example: The prime meridian passes through Greenwich, England.

keyWords.definition: a very accurate clock, especially one used for navigation at sea
keyWords.example: Sailors once relied on a chronometer to calculate their longitude.

keyWords.definition: the quality of being very exact and accurate
keyWords.example: The engineer measured the part with great precision.

keyWords.definition: to cross or meet at a point
keyWords.example: The two roads intersect near the old bridge.

keyWords.definition: relating to the finding of a route or position
keyWords.example: The ship's crew checked their navigational instruments before setting sail.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Only sailors from past centuries ever needed latitude and longitude, and no one uses them today
The prime meridian is the single most important place on Earth, and every city lies on it
Latitude and longitude form a grid that GPS now lets us use with great precision
Atomic clocks are useful only for telling the time of day, and not for maps or GPS
questions.why: The article traces how latitude and longitude create a coordinate grid, how that grid was historically hard to use, and how GPS now makes it precise and fast.

wrong.A: Modern travelers and GPS devices still depend on the same system.
wrong.B: The meridian is a reference line, not described as the most important place.
wrong.D: Atomic clocks are shown enabling GPS precision, not just telling time.

questions.stem: What does the article say made longitude historically difficult to calculate at sea?
options: A complete absence of any maps showing latitude, so that sailors could not find their place on the sea
Sailors' flat refusal to use any mathematics on the ship, because they thought it was a waste of time
A lack of stars that sailors could ever see at night, since the sky over the sea was always full of clouds
The need for an extremely precise chronometer that could withstand a rocking ship
questions.why: The article explains that calculating longitude required a chronometer precise enough to keep time while rocking at sea.

wrong.A: Maps and latitude lines are described as long-established.
wrong.B: Mathematics is implied as necessary, not refused.
wrong.C: Stars helped sailors find latitude, and were visible at sea.

questions.stem: According to the article, what role did the year 1884 play?
options: It is when chronometers were formally banned from all ships at sea
It is when the prime meridian was officially designated at Greenwich
It is when GPS satellites were first launched into orbit around Earth
It is when the equator was first discovered by explorers on a ship
questions.why: The article states the prime meridian was officially designated in 1884, running through Greenwich, England.

wrong.A: Chronometers were adopted for navigation, not banned.
wrong.C: GPS satellites are a much later, modern development.
wrong.D: The equator is not described as being 'discovered' in that year.

questions.stem: In the article, the word precision most nearly means —
options: the quality of being very exact and accurate
the distance measured between two separate oceans
a particular type of signal sent by a satellite
the feeling of being completely lost at sea
questions.why: The article repeatedly emphasizes how GPS and coordinates allow locations to be pinpointed with great precision, meaning exactness.

wrong.B: Ocean distance is unrelated to the word's meaning.
wrong.C: Precision is a quality, not a type of signal itself.
wrong.D: Being lost is the opposite of what precision describes.

questions.stem: Why does a GPS receiver need to communicate with a network of satellites?
options: Because only one single satellite exists in all of orbit around Earth
Because satellites must take turns passing above the equator each day
Because multiple satellite signals together calculate an exact position
Because one satellite alone would give the wrong time of day
questions.why: The article describes GPS as communicating with a network, implying several satellite signals combine to pinpoint an exact position.

wrong.A: The article refers to a network, meaning many satellites.
wrong.B: No such turn-taking over the equator is mentioned.
wrong.D: Time of day is not the function described for satellites.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why coordinates are often divided into minutes and seconds?
options: To decide exactly which country owns a given ocean or sea
To give an even more exact position than whole degrees alone
To measure how hot or cold a given location is on the map
To tell sailors on board precisely what time it is each day
questions.why: Since degrees alone cover large areas, subdividing into minutes and seconds allows for the extra precision the article emphasizes throughout.

wrong.A: Ocean ownership is not discussed in the article.
wrong.C: Temperature is unrelated to coordinate precision.
wrong.D: Minutes and seconds here are units of angle, not clock time.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the article's comparison of old and new navigation?
options: Navigation has grown far more precise since the days of early sailors
GPS cannot ever work without a coastline nearby to guide the ships
Chronometers are no longer useful for any purpose at all
Stars were always more reliable than any modern satellite
questions.why: The article contrasts centuries of difficulty finding longitude with GPS finding exact coordinates within seconds almost anywhere, showing great improvement.

wrong.B: GPS is shown working in remote deserts and open ocean, away from coastlines.
wrong.C: Chronometers are presented as a historical solution, not dismissed entirely.
wrong.D: GPS is presented as far more precise than star-based estimates.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly structured?
options: It argues that GPS devices should fully replace paper maps
It tells a fictional story about one explorer who got lost
It lists several dangers that modern sailors still face today
It defines the two lines, then traces their history into modern GPS
questions.why: The article moves from defining the two kinds of lines, to how they intersect to form coordinates, to the historical struggle with longitude, to GPS today.

wrong.A: The article does not argue against paper maps.
wrong.B: No fictional story is included.
wrong.C: Dangers to sailors are not listed.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why determining longitude was historically much harder than determining latitude, and how modern technology solved that problem. Use the words chronometer and precision.
checklist: I explained why longitude was hard to measure in the past.
I explained how GPS solved the problem.
I used chronometer and precision correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Determining longitude was historically difficult because, unlike latitude, which navigators could estimate from the stars, it required an exceptionally accurate chronometer capable of keeping correct time even while a ship rocked on the open sea for months. Modern technology solved this problem with GPS, where a receiver communicates with a network of orbiting satellites and calculates an exact position with remarkable precision within seconds, something early navigators relying on a chronometer alone could never have achieved.
